newsitem.title: USA: '92 magic missing for White House hopeful Perot.
newsitem.headline: '92 magic missing for White House hopeful Perot.

text.p: Ross Perot, the self-made Texas billionaire who turned U.S. politics upside down in 1992, has faltered this year -- his reformist plank tarnished by an autocratic style that has turned some supporters off.

Perot, 66, has run as nominee of the Reform Party -- his own creation -- on a promise to end the power of special interest groups in Washington and form a team of professionals to tackle the budget deficit, reform the Social Security old-age pension system and renegotiate foreign trade pacts.

But while the message is much the same as four years ago, when he won a strong 19 percent of the vote against winner Bill Clinton and then-President George Bush, Perot's 1996 campaign has seldom exceeded 5 or 6 percent in opinion polls.

Many voters, including some who backed him before, say they are put off by Perot -- whose blunt, assertive style strikes some as feisty and honest but others as overbearing and egotistical -- even if they like his ideas.
His campaign started badly with a bitter fight against former Colorado Gov. Richard Lamm for the nomination of the independent Reform Party that Perot set up with his own money.

Lamm was promised a fair race but complained that Perot aides blocked him from making his case to party members. The episode persuaded many that Perot, who made his name in the dog-eat-dog world of big business, was an autocrat ill-suited to the consensus-building central to the art of politics.
"He can't compromise," said Gerald Posner, who has published a biography of Perot. "He would be in Washington telling everyone what to do. You can't do that."

Many of the questions surrounding Perot's volatile temperament first surfaced in 1992, when he claimed to be the victim of several ill-defined conspiracies. He quit the race in mid-summer only to return in the fall.
This year he has been unable to stir much enthusiasm for his messianic promise to "return this country to the people".

"Perot came out of 1992 as tarnished goods and the dynamics of this campaign didn't set him up for serious consideration," said Curtis Gans, director of the nonpartisan Committee for the Study of the American Electorate.
Gans said the anti-establishment anger that fuelled Perot's cause in 1992 is not as strong a factor this year.

Perot's half-hour television pitches, complete with his trademark economic charts and graphs, have drawn much lower ratings than four years ago. His folksy wisecracks, delivered in a high-pitched Texas twang, sound less compelling now.

Perot's cause suffered a huge blow when Clinton and Republican Bob Dole agreed to exclude him from their two campaign debates, robbing him of a golden opportunity to grill them before a nationwide TV audience on the economic issues he sees as his main strength.
He angrily accused both men of freezing him out in order to "hand out free candy" rather than address hard issues.

Although he had early on aimed most of his campaign invective at Dole, as the instigator in the move to bar him from the debates, he has since launched furious attacks on Clinton's ethics and claims the president may face Watergate style crises in a second term.
It was action, not words, that created the Perot legend.
He became an American folk hero in 1979 by running a daring mission to rescue two of his imprisoned employees from revolution-torn Iran.
Born on June 27, 1930, in the small Texas town of Texarkana, near the Arkansas border, he is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy, where he first learned about computers.
He resigned from the Navy in 1957 to try his luck as a computer salesman for IBM and six years later put up $1,000 to register his own company, Electronic Data Systems Inc.

That company made him a paper billionaire by the time he was 38 and, when General Motors bought the Dallas-based company in 1984, Perot became the largest single shareholder of the world's largest corporation.

But he quickly clashed with top GM officials and was two years later paid $900 million to give up his seat on the GM board and relinquish control of EDS. He later set up a new company, Perot Systems, and his estimated fortune now stands at about $3.3 billion.
A devoted family man, Perot has been married to Margot Birmingham for 40 years and they have five children.
